p.src: When Jin Xuan heard that Zhang Fei was approaching with an army, he assembled his officers, mustered his best troops and weapons, and marched out of the city to meet the enemy. His aide Gong Zhi remonstrated: “Liu Xuande is an imperial uncle of the great Han, and his benevolence and righteousness are renowned throughout the realm. Moreover, Zhang Yide is a warrior of extraordinary valor. We must not meet him in battle; submission is our best course.” Jin Xuan flew into a rage. “Do you mean to collude with the rebels and betray me from within?” He shouted for the guards to drag Gong Zhi out and behead him. All the officials pleaded, “To execute one of your own officers before battle would bode ill for the army.”

p.src: Jin Xuan therefore dismissed Gong Zhi with an angry rebuke and personally led his army out. Twenty li from the city, he came face-to-face with Zhang Fei. Zhang Fei leveled his spear from horseback and roared a challenge at Jin Xuan. Jin Xuan asked his commanders, “Who dares go out and fight him?” They were all afraid, and none dared advance. Jin Xuan himself spurred forward, brandishing his saber to meet Zhang Fei. Zhang Fei gave a roar like a tremendous thunderclap. Jin Xuan turned pale and, not daring to engage, wheeled his horse and fled. Zhang Fei led his troops in a sweeping pursuit. When Jin Xuan reached the city walls, a storm of arrows shot down from above. He looked up in alarm and saw Gong Zhi standing on the wall, saying, “You defied Heaven’s hour and brought ruin upon yourself. The people and I have surrendered to Liu Bei.”

p.src: Now Han Xuan, governor of Changsha, had always been hot-tempered and quick to kill, and everyone hated him. When he learned that Yunchang’s army had arrived, he summoned the veteran general Huang Zhong to confer. Huang Zhong said, “My lord need not worry. With this saber and this bow of mine, though a thousand come, a thousand shall die!” Huang Zhong could in fact draw a bow of two shi and hit his mark with every shot. Before he had finished, a man below the steps stepped forward and declared, “There is no need for the old general to go into battle. I shall certainly capture this fellow Guan alive with my own hands.” Han Xuan looked and saw that it was Yang Ling, a commandant in charge of the troops. Han Xuan was delighted and ordered Yang Ling to lead a thousand men in a swift dash out of the city. After traveling about fifty li, they saw dust rising in the distance: Yunchang’s troops had already arrived. Yang Ling rode out with leveled spear and stood before the ranks, shouting insults and challenges. Yunchang was enraged. Without another word, he spurred his horse, whirled his blade, and charged straight at Yang Ling. Yang Ling leveled his spear and met him. Before three bouts had passed, Yunchang’s arm rose and his blade fell, cutting Yang Ling down from his horse. He pursued the routed troops all the way to the city walls.

p.src: When Han Xuan heard of this, he was greatly alarmed and ordered Huang Zhong to ride out. Han Xuan himself went up onto the city wall to watch. Huang Zhong took up his saber, mounted his horse, and led five hundred cavalrymen racing across the drawbridge. Seeing an old general ride out, Yunchang knew it was Huang Zhong. He drew up his five hundred saber-bearing guards in a single line, halted with blade held crosswise, and asked, “Can the approaching general be Huang Zhong?” Huang Zhong replied, “Since you know my name, how dare you trespass upon my territory?” Yunchang said, “I have come expressly to take your head!” With that, their horses met, and they fought for more than a hundred bouts without either gaining the advantage. Fearing that Huang Zhong might come to harm, Han Xuan sounded the gong to recall his forces. Huang Zhong withdrew his troops into the city. Yunchang also withdrew and encamped ten li from the city, thinking to himself, “The veteran Huang Zhong truly deserves his fame. In a hundred bouts he showed not the slightest opening. Tomorrow I must use the feigned-retreat blade stroke and cut him down from behind.” The next day, after the morning meal, he returned beneath the walls to issue another challenge. Han Xuan sat atop the wall and ordered Huang Zhong to ride out. Huang Zhong led several hundred horsemen charging across the drawbridge and once more engaged Yunchang. They fought another fifty or sixty bouts, with neither emerging the victor. Both armies cheered them in unison.

p.src: Just as the drums were pounding fiercely, Yunchang wheeled his horse and fled. Huang Zhong pursued him. Just as Yunchang was about to turn his blade upon him, he suddenly heard a crash behind his head. He looked back at once and saw that Huang Zhong’s warhorse had stumbled, throwing its rider to the ground. Yunchang promptly turned his horse, raised his blade in both hands, and roared, “For now I shall spare your life! Quickly change horses and come fight me again!” Huang Zhong hurriedly lifted the horse’s forelegs, sprang into the saddle, and galloped back into the city. Han Xuan questioned him in alarm, and Huang Zhong answered, “This horse has not been in battle for a long time; that is why it stumbled.” Han Xuan said, “Your arrows never miss. Why did you not shoot him?” Huang Zhong replied, “When we fight again tomorrow, I shall feign defeat, lure him to the drawbridge, and shoot him there.” Han Xuan gave Huang Zhong a gray horse from his own stable. Huang Zhong bowed his thanks and withdrew, thinking, “How rare is such honor and generosity as Yunchang’s! He could not bear to kill me; how could I bear to shoot him? Yet if I do not shoot, I fear I shall be disobeying a military command.” All that night he wavered, unable to decide.

p.src: At dawn the next day, word came that Yunchang was issuing a challenge. Huang Zhong led his troops out of the city. Unable to defeat Huang Zhong after two days of battle, Yunchang was extremely agitated. Summoning all his martial might, he engaged Huang Zhong once more. Before they had fought thirty bouts, Huang Zhong feigned defeat, and Yunchang pursued him. Remembering how Yunchang had spared his life the previous day, Huang Zhong could not bear to shoot him. He secured his saber, drew the bow without an arrow, and let the string twang. Yunchang dodged hastily, but no arrow appeared. Yunchang resumed the chase, and Huang Zhong once more loosed an empty string. Yunchang dodged again, but still there was no arrow. Thinking Huang Zhong did not know how to shoot, he pursued without concern. As they neared the drawbridge, Huang Zhong nocked an arrow and drew his bow upon the bridge. The string sounded, the arrow flew, and struck precisely at the base of the tassel on Yunchang’s helmet. The troops ahead raised a great shout in unison. Yunchang was startled and returned to camp with the arrow still lodged there. Only then did he realize that Huang Zhong possessed the skill to pierce a willow leaf at a hundred paces, and that by striking only his helmet tassel today, the old general had repaid the mercy shown him the day before.

p.src: Guan Yu led his troops away. Huang Zhong returned to the city and went to see Han Xuan, who at once shouted for his attendants to seize him. Huang Zhong cried, “I am innocent!” Han Xuan said in a fury, “I have watched you for three days. How dare you deceive me! The day before yesterday you did not fight with all your strength; you must have harbored private designs. Yesterday, when your horse stumbled, he did not kill you; there must be secret dealings between you. Today you twice drew an empty bow, yet your third arrow struck the tassel of his helmet exactly. How can this be anything but collusion between those outside and within? Unless I behead you, you will surely bring trouble hereafter!” He ordered the executioners to drag Huang Zhong beyond the city gate and behead him. The officers were about to plead for him, but Han Xuan said, “Anyone who asks that Huang Zhong be spared shall share his guilt!” They had just dragged him outside the gate and were about to raise the blade when an officer suddenly charged in, brandishing his sword. He cut down the executioner, rescued Huang Zhong, and cried, “Huang Hansheng is the bulwark of Changsha. To kill Hansheng is to kill the people of Changsha! Han Xuan is cruel and inhumane; he scorns the worthy and insults good men. Let us all put him to death! All who will follow me, come now!”

p.src: The people looked at the man. His face was the color of a ripe date and his eyes shone like bright stars. He was Wei Yan, a native of Yiyang. He had pursued Liu Xuande from Xiangyang but failed to catch up with him, and so had come to serve Han Xuan. Han Xuan had disliked his arrogance and lack of courtesy and refused to employ him in an important post, so he had languished here in obscurity. That day, after rescuing Huang Zhong, he called on the people to join him in killing Han Xuan. He bared his arm and gave one shout, and more than a hundred rallied to him. Huang Zhong was unable to restrain them. Wei Yan fought his way straight to the top of the city wall and cut Han Xuan in two with a single stroke. Carrying Han Xuan’s head, he mounted his horse, led the people out of the city, and went to submit to Guan Yu. Guan Yu was delighted. He entered the city, completed the work of reassuring the people, and asked to meet Huang Zhong. Huang Zhong pleaded illness and would not come out. Guan Yu immediately sent men to invite Xuande and Kongming.

p.src: Xuande treated Huang Zhong with great generosity. Guan Yu brought Wei Yan in to be presented, but Kongming shouted for the executioners to drag him away and behead him. Startled, Xuande asked Kongming, “Wei Yan is a man of merit and has committed no crime. Why does the military adviser wish to kill him?” Kongming replied, “To receive a lord’s stipend and then kill that lord is disloyal; to dwell in his land and then offer that land to another is unrighteous. I see the bone of rebellion at the back of Wei Yan’s head. In time he will surely revolt. Therefore I would behead him now and root out the cause of future calamity.” Xuande said, “If we kill this man, I fear that every other officer who has submitted will feel imperiled. I ask the military adviser to pardon him.” Pointing at Wei Yan, Kongming said, “For now I shall spare your life. Serve your lord with the utmost loyalty and entertain no rebellious thoughts. If such thoughts arise, I shall have your head, come what may.” Wei Yan repeatedly murmured assent and withdrew. Huang Zhong recommended Liu Pan, Liu Biao’s nephew, who was then living in retirement in You County. Xuande summoned him and placed him in charge of Changsha Commandery. With all four commanderies pacified, Xuande withdrew his army to Jingzhou and renamed Youjiangkou as Gong’an. From that time onward, money and grain were abundant, and worthy men came to join him; his generals and troops were dispersed to garrison the strategic passes.

p.src: Meanwhile, after Zhou Yu returned to Chaisang to recover from his illness, he ordered Gan Ning to guard Baling Commandery and Ling Tong to guard Hanyang Commandery. Warships were deployed at both places to await orders. Cheng Pu led the remaining officers and soldiers to Hefei County. It happened that ever since the fierce fighting at Red Cliffs, Sun Quan had long remained at Hefei, engaging Cao Cao’s forces in more than ten battles large and small without either side prevailing. Not daring to pitch camp close beneath the walls, he had stationed his army fifty li from the city. When he heard that Cheng Pu’s troops had arrived, Sun Quan was overjoyed and personally left the camp to welcome and reward them. Someone reported that Lu Zijing had arrived first. Sun Quan dismounted and stood waiting for him, whereupon Lu Su hastily rolled out of his saddle, dismounted, and saluted. The officers were all greatly astonished to see Sun Quan treat Lu Su in this manner. Sun Quan asked Lu Su to remount, and as they rode side by side, he said privately, “Was my dismounting to welcome you enough to display your distinction?” Lu Su replied, “Not yet.” Sun Quan asked, “Then what must happen before you are truly distinguished?” Lu Su replied, “I pray that my lord’s might and virtue may spread throughout the four seas, that you may unite all nine provinces and accomplish the work of an emperor. Then, when my name is inscribed in the annals, I shall at last be distinguished.”

Someone reported that Lu Zijing had arrived first. Sun Quan dismounted and stood waiting for him, whereupon Lu Su hastily rolled out of his saddle, dismounted, and saluted.
The officers were all greatly astonished to see Sun Quan treat Lu Su in this manner.
Sun Quan asked Lu Su to remount, and as they rode side by side, he said privately, “Was my dismounting to welcome you enough to display your distinction?”
Lu Su replied, “Not yet.”
Sun Quan asked, “Then what must happen before you are truly distinguished?”

Lu Su replied, “I pray that my lord’s might and virtue may spread throughout the four seas, that you may unite all nine provinces and accomplish the work of an emperor. Then, when my name is inscribed in the annals, I shall at last be distinguished.”

p.src: Sun Quan clapped his hands and laughed heartily. Together they entered the command tent, where he held a great banquet to reward the soldiers who had fought so fiercely, and they discussed a plan for taking Hefei. Suddenly a report came that Zhang Liao had sent a man with a letter of challenge. Sun Quan opened and read the letter, then said furiously, “Zhang Liao insults me beyond endurance! You heard that Cheng Pu’s army had arrived, and so deliberately sent someone to challenge me! Tomorrow I shall face you without using the new troops. Watch me fight a great battle!” He issued orders that at the fifth watch that night the entire army was to leave camp and advance toward Hefei. Around the hour of the dragon, when the army was halfway there, Cao Cao’s forces arrived, and the two sides drew up their battle lines. Sun Quan rode forth in a golden helmet and golden armor, fully arrayed for battle. Song Qian stood on his left and Jia Hua on his right; both wielded ornamented halberds and guarded him from either side. After the drums had sounded three times, the gate banners in Cao Cao’s ranks parted, and three generals, fully armed and belted, stood before the formation: Zhang Liao in the center, Li Dian on the left, and Yue Jin on the right. Zhang Liao spurred his horse to the front and challenged Sun Quan alone to single combat. Sun Quan grasped his spear and was about to fight in person when a general charged out early from the battle gate, spear leveled and horse at full gallop. It was Taishi Ci. Zhang Liao flourished his saber and met him. The two generals fought for seventy or eighty bouts without either gaining the advantage. In Cao Cao’s formation, Li Dian said to Yue Jin, “The man opposite us in the golden helmet is Sun Quan. If we capture Sun Quan, we can fully avenge the army of eight hundred and thirty thousand.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, Yue Jin, alone on one horse with one saber, charged diagonally at Sun Quan. Like a bolt of lightning he flew before him and brought down his blade. Song Qian and Jia Hua hurriedly raised their ornamented halberds to block him. Wherever the saber struck, both halberds broke at once, and they could only beat at his horse’s head with the broken shafts. Yue Jin wheeled his horse away, and Song Qian snatched a spear from a soldier’s hand and pursued him. Li Dian nocked an arrow and shot Song Qian squarely through the chest. Song Qian fell from his horse as the bowstring sounded. Seeing someone fall from a horse behind him, Taishi Ci abandoned Zhang Liao and turned back toward his own formation. Zhang Liao seized the advantage and swept forward in pursuit. The Wu troops fell into confusion and fled in every direction. Zhang Liao caught sight of Sun Quan and spurred his horse after him. Just as he was about to catch him, a force burst out obliquely. The great general at its head was Cheng Pu. After a sharp clash, Cheng Pu rescued Sun Quan. Zhang Liao gathered his troops and returned to Hefei.

p.src: Cheng Pu escorted Sun Quan back to the main camp, and the defeated troops returned one after another. When Sun Quan saw that Song Qian had been lost, he burst into loud weeping. Chief Secretary Zhang Hong said, “My lord relies upon the vigor of youth and treats a formidable enemy lightly, leaving every man in the army disheartened. To slay generals, seize banners, and make one’s might resound across the battlefield is the duty of a subordinate commander, not conduct befitting my lord. I beg you to restrain the valor of Meng Ben and Xia Yu and instead cherish the designs of a king and hegemon. Moreover, Song Qian’s death today amid blade and arrow was entirely the result of my lord’s underestimating the enemy. From now on, you must take the greatest care of yourself.” Sun Quan said, “The fault was mine. From now on, I shall amend my ways.”

p.src: Before long, Taishi Ci entered the command tent and said, “One of my men, Ge Ding, has a brother serving as a stable hand under Zhang Liao. That stable hand bears a grudge after being punished. Tonight he sent word that he will set a fire as a signal and assassinate Zhang Liao, thereby avenging Song Qian. I ask leave to lead troops in support from outside.” Sun Quan asked, “Where is Ge Ding?” Taishi Ci replied, “He has already slipped into Hefei. I beg five thousand troops for the undertaking.” Zhuge Jin said, “Zhang Liao is full of stratagems and may well be prepared. We must not act rashly.” Taishi Ci persisted in his resolve to go. Grieving over Song Qian’s death and eager to avenge him, Sun Quan therefore ordered Taishi Ci to lead five thousand troops in support of the plot.

p.src: Now Ge Ding was a fellow townsman of Taishi Ci. That day he mingled with the soldiers and followed them into Hefei, where he sought out the stable hand, and the two conferred. Ge Ding said, “I have already sent word to General Taishi Ci. He will surely come to support us tonight. How will you set about it?” The stable hand replied, “This place is rather far from the main camp, so we cannot force our way in swiftly at night. I shall simply set fire to a haystack, while you go to the front and cry rebellion. Once the soldiers in the city are thrown into confusion, we will take the opportunity to assassinate Zhang Liao, and the rest of his army will flee of itself.” Ge Ding said, “An excellent plan!”

p.src: That night Zhang Liao returned victorious to the city, rewarded the entire army for its efforts, and issued orders that no one was to remove his armor to sleep. Those around him said, “We won a complete victory today, and the troops of Wu have fled far away. Why do you not remove your armor and rest, General?” Zhang Liao replied, “That is not so. The way of a commander is neither to rejoice in victory nor grieve at defeat. If the troops of Wu suppose us unprepared and strike while we are vulnerable, how shall we meet them? Tonight our defenses must be more vigilant than on any other night.” Before he had finished speaking, fire broke out in the rear camp. Cries of rebellion rose everywhere, and messengers came streaming in one after another. Zhang Liao left his tent, mounted his horse, summoned several dozen trusted officers, and took his stand across the road. His attendants said, “The cries are most urgent. We should go and see what is happening.” Zhang Liao said, “How could the whole city have rebelled? The rebels are merely trying to throw the soldiers into alarm. Behead anyone who causes disorder!”

p.src: Before long, Li Dian brought Ge Ding and the stable hand before him in bonds. Zhang Liao questioned them and learned the truth of the affair. He had them beheaded at once before his horse. Just then, gongs and drums sounded outside the city gates, and tremendous battle cries arose. Zhang Liao said, “These are the Wu troops coming to support the rebels. We can turn their own scheme against them and defeat them.” He then ordered a fire lit inside the city gate. Everyone cried rebellion, the gates were flung wide open, and the drawbridge was lowered.

p.src: Seeing the city gates standing wide open, Taishi Ci assumed the uprising had begun within. Leveling his spear, he spurred his horse and charged in first. At a cannon shot from the walls, a storm of arrows rained down. Taishi Ci hastily retreated, but several arrows struck him. From behind, Li Dian and Yue Jin came charging out. More than half the Wu troops were lost, and the enemy pursued their advantage all the way to the front of the camp. Lu Xun and Dong Xi charged out, rescued Taishi Ci, and the troops of Cao withdrew. When Sun Quan saw Taishi Ci gravely wounded, his grief deepened. Zhang Zhao urged Sun Quan to abandon the campaign. Sun Quan agreed. He withdrew his troops, embarked them on the ships, and returned to Nanxu and Runzhou. By the time the troops and horses had settled into camp, Taishi Ci’s condition had grown grave. Sun Quan sent Zhang Zhao and others to inquire after him. Taishi Ci cried aloud, “A true man born into an age of chaos should bear a three-foot sword and accomplish deeds unequalled in history; yet now, before my ambition has been fulfilled, how can I die!” With those words he died, at the age of forty-one. p.src: Meanwhile, Xuande was drilling and reorganizing his forces in Jingzhou. When he heard that Sun Quan had been defeated at Hefei and had returned to Nanxu, he consulted Kongming. Kongming said, “Last night, while observing the stars, I saw a star fall to earth in the northwest. It surely portends the death of one of the imperial clan.”

p.src: Even as he spoke, a sudden report arrived that young lord Liu Qi had died of illness. When Xuande heard the news, he wept bitterly without cease. Kongming consoled him, saying, “Life and death are ordained. My lord, do not grieve, lest you harm your honored person. Attend instead to affairs of state. You should send someone there at once to guard the city and also arrange the funeral.” Xuande asked, “Who can be sent?” Kongming replied, “No one but Yunchang will do.” He immediately had Yunchang depart to defend Xiangyang. Xuande said, “Now that Liu Qi is dead, Eastern Wu will surely come to demand Jingzhou. How shall we answer them?” Kongming replied, “If anyone comes, I shall know how to answer him.” Half a month later, a man reported that Lu Su and others from Eastern Wu had come to offer condolences.
